subject: biology

questions.content: What is classification in biology?
options: Sorting living things into groups based on similarities
questions.explanation: Classification organises living things into groups according to shared features, which makes them easier to study and identify.

questions.content: Which is the correct order of classification groups from largest to smallest?
options: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom
Kingdom, class, phylum, order, genus, family, species
Phylum, kingdom, class, family, order, species, genus
questions.explanation: The taxonomic hierarchy goes from the broadest group, kingdom, down to the most specific, species.

questions.content: Which group of organisms are vertebrates that have feathers and lay eggs?
questions.explanation: Birds are the only vertebrates with feathers. They are warm-blooded and lay hard-shelled eggs.

questions.content: What is a species?
options: A group of organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring
A group of organisms living in the same place
questions.explanation: A species is a group of similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

questions.content: Which is a feature of all mammals?
options: They have fur or hair and feed milk to their young
questions.explanation: Mammals have hair or fur and produce milk from mammary glands to feed their young.

questions.content: In the binomial system the name Homo sapiens is used for humans. What does the first word represent?
questions.explanation: In binomial naming, the first word, with a capital letter, is the genus. The second, in lower case, is the species. Both are italicised or underlined.

questions.content: Why do scientists use binomial names instead of common names?
options: Binomial names are the same worldwide and avoid confusion
questions.explanation: Common names vary between languages and places, and one name can refer to different species. A binomial name identifies exactly one species.

questions.content: Which feature is used to separate arthropods into groups such as insects and arachnids?
options: Number of legs and body sections
questions.explanation: Insects have three pairs of legs and three body sections, whereas arachnids have four pairs of legs and two body sections.

questions.content: A dichotomous key is used to...
options: Identify an organism by answering a series of paired questions
Measure the biomass of a habitat
Count the number of species in an area
questions.explanation: A dichotomous key gives two choices at each step, based on observable features, leading step by step to the identity of the organism.

questions.content: Which characteristic do all fish share?
options: Gills for gas exchange and fins for movement
questions.explanation: Fish live in water, breathe with gills, and have fins. Most have scales and lay eggs.

questions.content: Which pair are both vertebrates?
questions.explanation: Frogs and snakes both have a backbone, so they are vertebrates. Spiders, crabs, worms, snails, jellyfish and starfish are invertebrates.

questions.content: Which kingdom contains organisms that feed by absorbing nutrients and have cell walls made of chitin?
questions.explanation: Fungi have chitin in their cell walls and feed by secreting enzymes and absorbing the products. Plants have cellulose cell walls.

questions.content: Which feature is used to place plants into the group called flowering plants?
options: They produce flowers and seeds enclosed in fruit
questions.explanation: Flowering plants (angiosperms) produce flowers, and their seeds develop inside a fruit. Ferns and mosses reproduce with spores.

questions.content: Two organisms share the same genus but belong to different species. What can you conclude?
options: They are closely related but cannot normally produce fertile offspring together
They are not related at all
questions.explanation: Members of the same genus share a recent common ancestor and many features, but by definition different species do not normally produce fertile offspring.

questions.content: A horse and a donkey can breed to produce a mule, which is sterile. What does this tell us about the horse and donkey?
questions.explanation: Because the offspring are infertile, the horse and donkey do not meet the species definition of producing fertile offspring, so they are separate species.

questions.content: Which is a limitation of classifying organisms only by appearance?
options: Unrelated organisms can look similar because of similar environments, and related ones can look different
questions.explanation: Convergent evolution can produce similar features in unrelated organisms. Modern classification also uses DNA and protein sequence evidence to show relationships.

questions.content: How does DNA analysis improve classification?
options: It compares base sequences to show how closely related organisms are
questions.explanation: The more similar the DNA base sequences of two organisms, the more recently they shared a common ancestor, which gives a more reliable picture of relationships.

questions.content: Using this key, identify organism X: 1a Has a backbone, go to 2. 1b No backbone, go to 4. 2a Has feathers, bird. 2b No feathers, go to 3. 3a Has fur, mammal. 3b Has scales, reptile. Organism X has a backbone, no feathers and scales. What is it?
questions.explanation: Following the key: backbone leads to 2, no feathers leads to 3, and scales gives reptile.

note:
Classification is the sorting of living things into groups based on similarities. There are millions of species on Earth, so scientists need a system that makes organisms easier to study, to name, and to identify, and that shows how closely related they are.

The hierarchy. The main groups form a hierarchy, from the largest and most general to the smallest and most specific: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Each smaller group sits inside the one above it. A useful way to remember the order is the phrase King Philip Came Over For Good Soup. The five kingdoms commonly used in school courses are animals, plants, fungi, protists and prokaryotes (bacteria). Viruses are not placed in any kingdom because they are not cells.

The species. A species is a group of organisms with similar features that can breed together to produce fertile offspring. A horse and a donkey can breed to produce a mule, but a mule is sterile, so a horse and a donkey are different species. The definition does not work perfectly for organisms that reproduce only asexually, or for fossils, so scientists also use structure and DNA.

Binomial naming. Each species has a two-part scientific name in Latin, the binomial system, introduced by Carl Linnaeus. The first part is the genus, written with a capital letter, and the second is the species, written in lower case. The whole name is italicised or underlined. For humans the name is Homo sapiens. Scientific names are the same across the world, unlike common names, which vary between languages and can refer to several different species.

Vertebrate groups. Vertebrates have a backbone and are divided into five classes. Fish have gills, fins and scales, and live in water. Amphibians have moist skin, lay eggs in water, and often live on land as adults. Reptiles have dry scaly skin and lay eggs with leathery shells on land. Birds have feathers, wings and beaks and lay hard-shelled eggs. Mammals have fur or hair, produce milk, and most give birth to live young.

Invertebrates have no backbone. Arthropods, the largest group, have jointed legs and an exoskeleton. They include insects with three pairs of legs and three body sections, arachnids with four pairs of legs and two body sections, crustaceans, and myriapods. Other invertebrate groups include molluscs, annelids (segmented worms), cnidarians such as jellyfish and echinoderms such as starfish.

Plants are divided into flowering plants, which produce seeds in fruits, conifers, which produce seeds in cones, and ferns and mosses, which reproduce using spores.

Keys. A dichotomous key is a tool for identifying an organism by answering a series of paired questions about observable features. Each step gives two choices, and each choice leads either to another question or to the name of the organism. To write a good key, use clear features that can be seen without special equipment, avoid features like size that vary, and make sure each question has only two answers.

Modern classification. Scientists used to classify mainly by structure. Features may look similar because of similar environments and not because of close relationship, for example the streamlined bodies of sharks and dolphins. Today, comparing DNA base sequences and protein sequences gives stronger evidence about how recently organisms shared a common ancestor, and some groupings have been revised as a result.

Exam tip: when using a key, write the step numbers you followed. When asked why binomial names are used, mention that they are universal and unique to one species.

flashcards.back: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
A group of similar organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring.
Two-part Latin name: genus (capital letter) then species (lower case), e.g. Homo sapiens.
They are universal and identify exactly one species, unlike common names.
Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.
Insect: 3 pairs of legs and 3 body sections. Arachnid: 4 pairs of legs and 2 body sections.
A key that identifies organisms by a series of paired questions with two choices each.

flashcards.front: Why is a mule evidence that horse and donkey are different species?
flashcards.back: Mules are sterile, so horses and donkeys do not produce fertile offspring together.
More similar base sequences mean closer relatedness and a more recent common ancestor.

subject: biology

questions.content: What is biodiversity?
options: The variety of living organisms in an area or on Earth
The mass of plants in a field
The number of animals in a zoo
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety of life, including the number of different species, the genetic variation within species and the variety of habitats.

questions.content: What is a quadrat used for?
options: Sampling plants or slow-moving animals in a defined area
questions.explanation: A quadrat is a square frame placed on the ground to count or estimate the cover of organisms in a known area.

questions.content: Which piece of equipment is used to catch small crawling invertebrates on the ground?
questions.explanation: A pitfall trap is a container sunk into the ground so that crawling invertebrates fall in and can be counted and identified.

questions.content: What is meant by a habitat?
options: The place where an organism lives
questions.explanation: A habitat is the place where an organism lives, which provides food, shelter and other needs.

questions.content: Why is random sampling important in a field study?
options: To avoid bias and make the sample representative
To make the study faster to write
To find only the rarest species
questions.explanation: Choosing sample positions randomly, for example with random coordinates, avoids bias and gives results that better represent the whole area.

questions.content: A student places 10 quadrats of area 0.25 square metres in a field and counts 60 daisies in total. What is the mean number of daisies per square metre?
questions.explanation: The total area sampled is 10 times 0.25, which is 2.5 square metres. Sixty daisies divided by 2.5 square metres is 24 daisies per square metre.

questions.content: A field has an area of 2,000 square metres and the mean density of clover is 8 per square metre. What is the estimated population of clover in the field?
questions.explanation: Population estimate equals mean density multiplied by total area, so 8 times 2,000 is 16,000.

questions.content: A transect is a line across a habitat. When is a transect better than random quadrats?
options: When conditions change gradually, such as from the shore up a beach
When the habitat is exactly the same everywhere
questions.explanation: A belt or line transect samples at regular intervals along an environmental gradient, so it shows how species distribution changes with conditions.

questions.content: In the capture-mark-release-recapture method, 40 animals are marked and released. A later sample of 50 includes 10 marked animals. What is the estimated population?
questions.explanation: Population equals (number marked first, 40) multiplied by (second sample, 50) divided by (marked in second sample, 10), which is 2,000 divided by 10, giving 200.

questions.content: Which assumption is needed for capture-mark-release-recapture to give a reliable estimate?
options: Marks do not harm the animals and the marked animals mix evenly with the population
The population grows during the study
questions.explanation: The method assumes that marking does not affect survival or behaviour, that marked individuals mix randomly, and that there is no major migration, birth or death during the study.

questions.content: Which sample would show higher biodiversity?
questions.explanation: Biodiversity depends on the number of species and how evenly individuals are distributed among them. Sample A has more species and an even spread.

questions.content: What is an indicator species?
options: A species whose presence or absence shows the condition of the environment
A species that is always rare
A species that is only in zoos
questions.explanation: Some species are sensitive to a factor such as pollution, so their presence or absence indicates environmental quality. Lichens indicate air quality and mayfly nymphs indicate clean water.

questions.content: Stonefly and mayfly nymphs are found in a stream, but only bloodworms are found downstream of a sewage outlet. What does this suggest?
options: Water downstream has low oxygen and is more polluted
The stream has more biodiversity downstream
questions.explanation: Stonefly and mayfly nymphs need well-oxygenated clean water. Bloodworms tolerate low oxygen, so their dominance suggests organic pollution.

questions.content: A student's ten quadrat counts are 4, 5, 4, 5, 5, 4, 6, 4, 5, 5 and a second student's ten counts are 1, 12, 3, 9, 0, 14, 2, 6, 0, 0. Both sets have the same mean of 4.7. What does this suggest?
options: The second set has much greater variation, so the species is distributed unevenly
The second set is more accurate
questions.explanation: The same mean can hide very different spreads. The second set has a large range, suggesting patchy distribution or a small number of samples that are not representative.

questions.content: Why does increasing the number of quadrats improve the reliability of an estimate?
options: A larger sample reduces the effect of chance and unusual areas on the mean
It removes the need for random placement
questions.explanation: More samples reduce the influence of unusual patches and chance variation, so the mean is closer to the true population density.

questions.content: Which sampling method is least suitable for estimating the population of fast-moving fish in a large lake?
options: Using a standardised trap at set sites
questions.explanation: Quadrats suit stationary organisms. Fast-moving or mobile animals need methods such as mark-recapture or trapping.

questions.content: Why is it important to monitor biodiversity over many years rather than just once?
options: To detect trends and changes caused by human activity or climate
To increase the number of species
questions.explanation: Populations vary naturally from year to year. Long-term monitoring separates real trends from natural fluctuation and shows whether conservation actions work.

questions.content: A survey finds that species richness in a wood is the same in two years but several rare species have been replaced by common ones. Why might the wood still be considered less biodiverse?
options: Biodiversity includes the uniqueness and evenness of species, not just the number
Common species lower the species count
questions.explanation: Replacing rare or specialised species with common generalists reduces the distinctiveness and evenness of the community, even if the total species count stays the same.

note:
Biodiversity means the variety of living things. It includes the number of different species in an area (species richness), the genetic variation within each species, and the variety of habitats and ecosystems. High biodiversity usually makes an ecosystem more stable and better able to cope with change, because more species means more ways for energy and nutrients to flow if one species declines.

Measuring biodiversity needs a method for sampling, because counting every organism in a habitat is impossible. A sample is a small, representative part of the whole. To avoid bias, sample positions are chosen at random, for example by using random coordinates on a grid. A bigger sample, and repeated samples, give more reliable estimates.

Quadrats are square frames, often 0.25 or 1 square metre, used for plants and slow-moving animals. The number of individuals is counted, or the percentage cover is estimated. If the area of each quadrat and the number placed are known, the mean number per square metre, the density, can be found by dividing the total count by the total area sampled. The population in a larger area can then be estimated by multiplying the mean density by the total area. For example, a mean of 8 clover plants per square metre in a field of 2,000 square metres suggests about 16,000 plants.

Transects are lines or belts laid across a habitat, with samples taken at regular intervals. They are best used when conditions change gradually, such as from a shaded woodland floor into an open meadow or up a rocky shore. They show how species distribution relates to an environmental factor such as light, moisture or salinity.

For animals, other methods are used. Pitfall traps catch crawling invertebrates. Pooters collect small insects from vegetation. Sweep nets collect insects from grass, and kick sampling is used in streams. For mobile animals, the capture-mark-release-recapture method is used. A first sample is caught, marked in a harmless way and released. After the animals have mixed with the population, a second sample is taken and the number of marked animals is counted. The population estimate is the number marked in the first sample multiplied by the size of the second sample, divided by the number of marked animals recaptured. The method assumes that marking does not harm the animals, that marked animals mix randomly, and that there are no major births, deaths or migration between samples.

Indicator species help to monitor the environment. Lichens vary in their sensitivity to sulfur dioxide, so the types present show air quality. Mayfly and stonefly nymphs need clean, oxygen-rich water, and bloodworms and sludge worms tolerate low oxygen, so the invertebrates in a stream indicate water pollution.

Analysing data. Calculate the mean and consider the spread, as the same mean can come from very different sets of values. Present results in tables and graphs, and discuss reliability, validity and possible errors. Ethical fieldwork means returning organisms to their habitat, leaving the area as found, and avoiding damage.

Monitoring over time. Populations vary naturally from year to year, so repeated surveys over many years are needed to see real trends. Long-term data show how biodiversity responds to climate change, pollution, habitat loss and conservation work. Citizen science projects collect large amounts of data from volunteers.

Exam tip: show your working for population estimates. State the formula, substitute the numbers, and include units.

flashcards.back: The variety of living things: number of species, genetic variation within species, and variety of habitats.
A square frame used to sample plants or slow-moving animals in a known area.
To avoid bias and make the sample representative of the whole area.
Mean density per square metre multiplied by the total area.
A line or belt across a habitat sampled at intervals, used when conditions change gradually.
Population = (number marked in first sample x size of second sample) divided by number of marked animals recaptured.
Marking does not harm; marked animals mix evenly; little birth, death or migration between samples.
A species whose presence or absence shows the condition of the environment, e.g. lichens for air quality.
To separate real trends from natural fluctuations and see effects of human activity or conservation.

subject: biology

questions.content: What does conservation mean?
options: Protecting and managing species and habitats
questions.explanation: Conservation is the protection and sustainable management of species, habitats and ecosystems.

questions.content: Which human activity is a major cause of habitat loss?
questions.explanation: Clearing forests for farming, timber and building destroys the habitats of many species.

questions.content: What is an endangered species?
options: A species at risk of becoming extinct
A species with a large population
A species that lives in water
questions.explanation: Endangered species have such small or declining populations that they are at serious risk of extinction.

questions.content: What is extinction?
options: When a species no longer exists anywhere
questions.explanation: A species is extinct when the last individual has died and it can never come back.

questions.content: Which gas released by burning fossil fuels contributes to climate change?
questions.explanation: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.

questions.content: Which is an example of an in situ conservation method?
options: Creating a national park to protect a habitat
Storing seeds in a seed bank
questions.explanation: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat, for example in reserves and national parks. Zoos and seed banks are ex situ.

questions.content: Which is an example of an ex situ conservation method?
options: A seed bank storing seeds from rare plants
questions.explanation: Ex situ conservation takes organisms or their genetic material out of their natural habitat, as in zoos, botanic gardens and seed banks.

questions.content: How do captive breeding programmes help endangered species?
options: They increase numbers and maintain genetic diversity, and animals can be reintroduced
They remove all predators from the world
questions.explanation: Zoos breed animals in a managed way to avoid inbreeding. Individuals may later be released to the wild if suitable habitat is available.

questions.content: Why can invasive species harm native biodiversity?
options: They may outcompete native species or prey on them as they have no natural predators
They increase the number of native species
questions.explanation: Non-native species introduced by humans may spread rapidly, compete for food and space, spread disease, or prey on natives.

questions.content: Overfishing is a threat to marine biodiversity. Which measure helps reduce it?
options: Setting fishing quotas and minimum net mesh sizes
Using smaller nets with larger numbers of boats
questions.explanation: Quotas limit the number of fish caught and larger mesh sizes let young fish escape, so fish stocks can recover and remain sustainable.

questions.content: Why can monoculture farming reduce biodiversity?
options: Growing a single crop over large areas removes habitats and food sources for many species
It increases the number of species
questions.explanation: Large areas of a single crop provide little variety of food or shelter, and pesticide use may harm non-target species.

questions.content: What is eutrophication?
options: Fertiliser runoff causes algal growth that depletes oxygen in water
A rise in oxygen in water
questions.explanation: Nutrients from fertilisers promote algal blooms. When algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up oxygen, so fish and other organisms die.

questions.content: Which of these is a sustainable practice in forestry?
options: Clearing a whole forest at once
questions.explanation: Sustainable forestry replaces harvested trees and protects habitats so that timber can be produced without long-term damage.

questions.content: Why is genetic diversity important in a small population of an endangered species?
options: It increases the chance that some individuals survive disease or environmental change
It reduces the number of offspring
questions.explanation: Greater genetic variation means a better chance that some individuals have alleles suited to new conditions, so the population can adapt. Small populations risk inbreeding.

questions.content: The removal of a keystone species such as a top predator can have large effects. Which is a likely effect?
options: Prey populations may increase and overgraze, changing the ecosystem
questions.explanation: Keystone species have effects on the ecosystem out of proportion to their numbers. Removing a top predator can cause prey to rise and damage vegetation and other species.

questions.content: A government bans trade in ivory. Which argument supports this action?
options: It reduces the demand and poaching that threaten elephant populations
questions.explanation: Legal protection and trade bans aim to cut poaching by reducing market demand, although enforcement and local community needs affect how well they work.

questions.content: A community near a reserve loses access to farmland. Which approach best balances conservation and local needs?
options: Involving the community in management and sharing benefits such as tourism income
Moving the reserve to another country
questions.explanation: Conservation is more successful when local people benefit, for example through jobs in ecotourism and sustainable use of resources, so they support protection.

questions.content: Which statement correctly links climate change to biodiversity loss?
options: Changing temperatures and rainfall alter habitats faster than some species can adapt or migrate
Climate change increases the number of habitats
Climate change has no link to species
questions.explanation: Warming alters habitats and timing of events such as flowering. Species that cannot adapt or move may decline, and coral reefs bleach when oceans warm and acidify.

note:
Human activity is changing the planet faster than ever before, and the result is a rapid loss of biodiversity. Conservation is the protection and sustainable management of species and habitats, so that they continue to exist and to provide the resources and services on which we depend.

Threats to biodiversity. Habitat loss is the biggest threat. Forests are cleared for farming, timber, mining and building, wetlands are drained, and land is divided into small fragments by roads. Pollution harms organisms: fertilisers that run off fields cause eutrophication, in which nutrients make algae grow rapidly, the algae then die and decompose, and bacteria use up the oxygen so that fish suffocate. Pesticides can kill non-target species, and plastic waste harms marine animals. Overexploitation, such as overfishing and hunting, reduces populations faster than they can recover. Invasive species introduced by people can outcompete or prey on native species that have no defence against them. Climate change, driven by the release of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels, changes temperature and rainfall, and species may be unable to adapt or move quickly enough. Warming and acidification of the oceans cause coral bleaching.

Why biodiversity matters. Ecosystems with greater biodiversity are usually more stable, because if one species declines, others can fill its role. Species provide food, medicines, materials and pollination, and ecosystems provide services such as clean water and carbon storage. Many people also believe that species have value in their own right. Genetic diversity is important within species: a population with more variation is more likely to include individuals that survive a new disease or a change in conditions, whereas small populations suffer inbreeding. Some species are keystone species, which have an effect on the ecosystem much larger than their numbers suggest. Removing a top predator, for example, can allow prey to overgraze and alter the whole community.

Conservation methods. In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat, through national parks, nature reserves, marine protected areas and wildlife corridors that connect fragments of habitat. Ex situ conservation takes organisms out of their habitat, as in zoos with captive breeding programmes, botanic gardens, and seed banks that store seeds of rare plants. Animals bred in captivity may be reintroduced to the wild if habitat is available and if the threat has been dealt with. Legal protection, such as bans on hunting or trade in ivory, and international agreements, such as CITES, regulate the trade in endangered species. Sustainable practices help too: fishing quotas and larger mesh nets protect fish stocks, forests can be replanted after felling, and farmers can keep hedgerows and rotate crops.

Balancing needs. Conservation can conflict with the needs of local people, for example if a reserve limits farmland. Programmes work best when local communities are involved and share the benefits, for example through ecotourism, and when people have alternative sources of income. Governments, businesses and individuals all have roles to play, from policy and regulation to choosing sustainably sourced products.

Exam tip: in an evaluation question, explain how a method works, give at least one advantage and one limitation, and mention the viewpoint of different stakeholders, such as conservationists, farmers and local communities.

flashcards.back: Protecting and sustainably managing species, habitats and ecosystems.
Habitat loss, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species and climate change.
Protecting species in their natural habitat, e.g. national parks and reserves.
Protecting species outside their habitat, e.g. zoos, botanic gardens and seed banks.
Fertiliser runoff causes algal blooms; decomposing algae use up oxygen and aquatic life dies.
A non-native species that spreads and harms native species by competition or predation.
A species with an effect on its ecosystem far larger than its numbers suggest.
It increases the chance that some individuals survive disease or environmental change.
Quotas, minimum net mesh size and protected breeding areas.
